hints: Count how the carbon skeleton changes when $\text{Br}$ leaves and the new carbon containing group joins, remember the new carbon counts in the longest chain.
walkthrough:
Follow the carbon chain**
You start with 1-bromobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{Br}$, which has 4 carbons. In this reaction the $\text{-Br}$ is swapped for $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$. That adds one extra carbon, so product A has 5 carbons in total with a nitrile group at the end. A 5 carbon nitrile is called pentanenitrile.
Final answer: pentanenitrile ($\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{CN}$)

hints: Think about the word nucleus loving, what kind of electron rich particle would be attracted to a slightly positive carbon atom?
walkthrough:
Picture what loves a nucleus**
A nucleophile loves positive charge. The carbon attached to bromine in $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{-Br}^{\delta-}$ is electron poor, so a nucleophile uses its own electron richness to attack it. That electron richness is a lone pair of electrons which it donates to form a new covalent bond.
Final answer: A species that donates a lone pair / electron pair to form a new covalent bond.

hints: Look at potassium cyanide dissolved in ethanol, which part is ionic and has a lone pair available to attack the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ atom?
walkthrough:
Split the reagent into its ions**
Potassium cyanide, $\text{KCN}$, dissolves to give $\text{K}^{+}$ and $\text{CN}^{-}$. The $\text{K}^{+}$ ion cannot donate electrons, but the cyanide ion has a lone pair on carbon and a negative charge. It is the electron pair donor that attacks the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$, so $\text{CN}^{-}$ is the nucleophile.
Final answer: $\text{CN}^{-}$ / cyanide ion

hints: Compare the reactant $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{Br}$ with the product $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{CN}$, what has left and what has taken its place on the same carbon?
walkthrough:
See the swap**
Substitution means one group takes the place of another on the same carbon. Here the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks and a new $\text{C-CN}$ bond forms on that same carbon atom: $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{Br} + \text{CN}^{-} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{CN} + \text{Br}^{-}$. Because $\text{Br}$ is directly replaced by $\text{CN}$, it is a substitution.
Final answer: The Br atom is replaced by the CN / nitrile group.

hints: To change $\text{-Br}$ into $\text{-NH}_2$, what nitrogen containing nucleophile could supply the $\text{NH}_2$ group?
Think why a sealed tube is needed when the nitrogen reagent is a gas that would escape on heating.
walkthrough:
Choose the nitrogen nucleophile**
You need to put $\text{-NH}_2$ where $\text{-Br}$ was: $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{NH}_2$. The nucleophile that delivers nitrogen is ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$. It donates its lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and displaces $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Trap the volatile reagent**
Ammonia is a gas and would escape if you just warmed it in an open flask. Heating it under pressure in a sealed tube keeps a high concentration of $\text{NH}_3$ around the halogenoalkane so substitution to the amine goes to completion.

Final answer: reagent(s): ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$, excess concentrated)
conditions: heat under pressure / heat in a sealed tube

hints: Use the times 460 s, 190 s and 40 s to order the speed of reaction, remember a shorter time means halide ion is released faster.
Link the speed to the bond that must break to release $\text{Cl}^{-}$, $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$, consider how bond length and strength change down Group 17.
walkthrough:
Read the times as rates**
A precipitate of $\text{AgX}$ only forms once $\text{X}^{-}$ has been released by hydrolysis. $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CI}$ takes only 40 s, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$ takes 190 s, and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}$ takes 460 s. Shorter time means faster release of halide, so reactivity order is chloride slowest, bromide middle, iodide fastest.

Explain with the bond that breaks**
The key step is breaking the $\text{C-X}$ bond. Going down Group 17 the halogen atom gets larger, the $\text{C-X}$ bond gets longer and weaker. $\text{C-Cl}$ is strongest, $\text{C-I}$ is weakest, so $\text{C-I}$ needs the least energy to break and reacts fastest. That is why the iodide precipitates first.

Final answer: Reactivity increases from Cl to Br to I, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl} < (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr} < (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CI}$.
This is because C-X bond strength decreases from C-Cl to C-Br to C-I, so less energy is needed to break the bond.

hints: Look at the structure $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CX}$, how many alkyl groups are joined to the carbon carrying the halogen?
Recall the two steps of $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$, which slow first step forms a positively charged carbon intermediate?
Think how methyl groups push electron density toward a positive centre and why that lowers energy.
walkthrough:
Classify the halogenoalkanes**
In $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CX}$ the carbon bonded to X is joined to three other carbons, three methyl groups. That makes each one a tertiary halogenoalkane. Tertiary systems strongly favour $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$.

See why $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ fits**
$\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ starts with the $\text{C-X}$ bond breaking on its own to give a carbocation: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-X} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^{+} + \text{X}^{-}$. This slow step needs a stable cation to be feasible.

Stabilise the positive charge**
Methyl groups are electron donating by the positive inductive effect. The three methyl groups push electron density onto the central $\text{C}^{+}$, spreading and stabilising the positive charge. This stable tertiary carbocation makes the $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ pathway low in energy and therefore favoured.

Final answer: All three are tertiary / $3^{\circ}$ halogenoalkanes.
The carbocation / intermediate formed is stable.
This is due to the electron donating / releasing effect (+I effect) of the three methyl groups attached to the central C.

hints: $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ needs a clear attack path for the nucleophile in one step, would a crowded tertiary carbon or an open carbon with little blocking be better?
walkthrough:
Choose the opposite crowding**
$\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ happens in one step with the nucleophile attacking the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ directly. It is fastest when the carbon is open with little blocking. A primary halogenoalkane such as 1-bromobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{Br}$, has only one alkyl group on that carbon, so attack is easy and $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ is favoured.
Final answer: Any primary halogenoalkane, e.g. 1-chlorobutane / 1-bromobutane / 1-iodobutane ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{X}$).
